(Section)

As for blessing (al-barakah), it likewise has two types:

The first: a blessing which is His action, may He be blessed and exalted. Its verb is bāraka, which is transitive by itself at times, by a particle "ʿalā" at times, and by a particle "fī" at times.

Its passive participle is mubārak, which is that which has been made so, and thus it is blessed by His making it so, may He be exalted.

The second type: a blessing which is attributed to Him as the attribution of mercy, might, and action, from which comes tabāraka (may He be blessed). For this reason that is not said of anyone else, and it is not fitting except for Him, mighty and majestic.

So He, glorified is He, is the Blessed (al-Mubārak), and His servant and messenger is blessed, as the Messiah, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And He has made me blessed wherever I may be﴾.

Whoever God blesses, and bestows blessing upon, is blessed. As for His attribute tabāraka, it is specific to Him, may He be exalted, as He applied it to Himself by His saying: ﴿Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds﴾; ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾; ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾; ﴿And blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned﴾; ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾; ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that﴾; ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾. Do you not see how it recurs throughout the Qur'an, applied to Him, specific to Him, not applied to anyone else? It comes in the pattern of amplitude and intensification, like taʿālā (exalted) and taʿāẓama (magnified) and the like, so the form tabāraka matches the form taʿālā, which indicates the perfection and utmost degree of loftiness. Thus tabāraka indicates the perfection of His blessing, its greatness and its vastness.

This is the meaning of the saying of some of the early scholars (al-salaf): "Tabāraka means He magnified Himself (taʿāẓama)."

Another said: "Its meaning is that blessings come from Him; all blessing is from Him."

Another said: "His good and His kindness to His creation increased."

It was said: "His compassion and mercy toward them expanded."

It was said: "He transcends everything in His attributes and His actions." And from here it was said: "Its meaning is taʿālā and taʿāẓama."

It was said: "Tabāraka means taqaddasa (He is sanctified), and holiness (al-qudus) is purity."

It was said: "Tabāraka means: by His name He blesses everything."

It was said: "Tabāraka means He is elevated, and al-mubārak is the one whose mention is elevated," related by al-Baghawi.

It was said: "Tabāraka means blessing is acquired and attained by mentioning Him."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "He brought every blessing."

It was said: "Its meaning is that He remained and endured in what has never ceased and will never cease, His remembrance," also by al-Baghawi.

The true meaning of the word is that barakah is abundance of good and its continuity, and no one is more deserving of this in attribute and action than Him, may He be blessed and exalted.

The early scholars' explanation revolves around these two meanings, and they are mutually entailing. But the more fitting meaning for the word is the meaning of attribute, not action, for it is an intransitive verb like taʿālā, taqaddasa, and taʿaẓẓama. Words of this kind do not mean that He made others high, holy, or great; this is something the word cannot bear in any way. Rather their meaning lies in the one to whom they are ascribed: He is the Exalted, the Holy.

Likewise, tabāraka cannot mean "He blessed others." How far one is from the other, in wording and meaning! This is intransitive and that is transitive. So you know that whoever explained tabāraka as "He cast blessing and blessed others" has not hit its meaning, although this is among the implications of His being blessed. Tabāraka is of the pattern of tamajjada, and majd is abundance of attributes of majesty, vastness and bounty; bāraka is of the pattern of aʿṭā and anʿama. Since the transitive form in this entails the intransitive without the converse, those early scholars who explained the word in the transitive sense did so to encompass both meanings, saying: "the coming of all blessing is from Him," or "all blessing is from Him." This is a branch of tabāraka in itself. We have fully discussed this in the book al-Fath al-Makki, where we explained that all blessing belongs to Him, may He be exalted, and from Him comes the one who is blessed; whoever He casts His blessing upon is blessed. For this reason His Book is blessed, His House is blessed, and the times and places He honored and singled out above others are blessed: the Night of Power is blessed, the surroundings of al-Aqsa are blessed, and the land of Sham He described as blessed in four or five places of His Book. Reflect on the words of the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith of Thawban, narrated by Muslim in his Sahih, when he turned from prayer:

"O God, You are Peace, and from You is peace. Blessed are You, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor."

Narrated by Muslim, Abu Dawud and Ahmad.

Reflect on how these noble words combine both kinds of praise: praise of transcendence and glorification, and praise of commendation and exaltation, in the most eloquent, concise and complete wording. He informed that He is Peace and from Him is peace. Peace belongs to Him in attribute and dominion, and the explanation of this was given earlier in discussing His attribute as al-Salam, and that His attributes of perfection, the descriptions of His majesty, His actions and His names are all peace. Likewise all praise belongs to Him in attribute and dominion; He is the Praised in His essence, and He makes whoever He wills among His servants praised, granting them praise from Him. Likewise all might belongs to Him in attribute and dominion; He is the Mighty than whom nothing is mightier, and whoever among His servants is made mighty is made so by His empowering him. Likewise all mercy belongs to Him in attribute and dominion. Likewise blessing: He is the Blessed in His essence, who blesses whom He wills of His creation, and thereby they become blessed: ﴿So blessed is God, Lord of the worlds﴾; ﴿And blessed is He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, and to Him you will be returned﴾.

This is a carpet (basāṭ, i.e., an open expanse for exploration), and the furthest the knowledge of scholars reaches is approaching its outer edges and borders. As for what lies beyond that, it is as the most knowledgeable of creation about God, the closest to God, and the most elevated in station with Him said: "I cannot count the praise upon You; You are as You have praised Yourself."

Narrated by Muslim.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 67, verse 2:

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad (Fudayl ibn 'Iyad) said: "It is the most sincere (akhlasuhu) and the most correct (asawbuhu)."

They said: "O Abu 'Ali, what is meant by 'most sincere' and 'most correct'?"

He said: "Indeed, a deed, if it is sincere but not correct, is not accepted. And if it is correct but not sincere, it is not accepted either, until it is both sincere and correct. Sincerity (al-ikhlas) means that it is for Allah, and correctness (al-sawab) means that it is in accordance with the Sunnah (the Prophetic way)."

Then he recited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 110].

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah while being a doer of good﴾ [al-Nisa: 125].

He, glorified is He, informed that He created the heavens and the earth, the upper and lower worlds, in order to test us as to which of us is best in deed.

He informed that He adorned the earth with what is upon it of animals, plants, minerals and other things for this test, and that He created death and life for this test.

So this test became the ultimate purpose of the creation and the command, and there was no escape from an abode in which this test takes place, and it is the abode of obligation (dar al-taklif).

And since it had preceded in His wisdom that Paradise is an abode of bliss, not an abode of trial and examination, He made before it the abode of trial as a bridge to cross over to it, a field in which to sow seed, and a harbor from which to take provision.

This is the truth for which and because of which creation was created: that He alone be worshipped by what He commanded through the tongues of His messengers. He commanded and forbade through the Sunnah, and He promised us reward and punishment. He did not create His creatures in vain, neither commanding them nor forbidding them, nor leaving them neglected, neither rewarding them nor punishing them. Rather, they were created for command and prohibition, for reward and punishment, and nothing other than this befits His wisdom and His praiseworthiness.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 67, verses 3–4:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You see no disparity in the creation of the Most Merciful﴾

Whatever disparity and lack of proportion exists goes back to the absence of giving proportion to the created thing. Proportion is an existential matter, connected to causation and originating creation. So whatever lacks it, lacks it because the Creator did not will proportion for it. That is a privative matter, for which the absence of origination and causation is sufficient. So reflect on this, for it will remove from you the difficulty in His saying: ﴿You see no disparity in the creation of the Most Merciful﴾.

Disparity occurs because proportion was not willed, just as ignorance, deafness, blindness, muteness and dumbness are sufficiently explained by the absence of the will to create and bring them into being.

**(Section)**

It should be known that things formed gradually from their matter, such as plants and animals, either have a deficiency arise in them, which is an evil, at their beginning or after their formation.

The first is when causes affect their matter that make it of poor temperament and deficient readiness, so that evil and deficiency occur in their creation through that cause. This is not because the Agent withheld from it and removed from it an existential thing by which it would be perfected. Rather, it is because the recipient did not accept perfection and completion, and its non-acceptance is a privative matter, not something from the Agent.

As for what comes from the Agent, it is the existential good by which the thing receives its perfection, completion and wholeness. The evil that occurs in it results from the lack of supplying it with the cause of perfection, so it remains in its original nonexistence.

By this, the secret of His saying is understood: ﴿You see no disparity in the creation of the Most Merciful﴾.

What He creates is an existential matter, through which the created thing has its perfection and completion. Its defect and deficiency come from its non-acceptance, and non-acceptance is not a created thing connected to the act of the Agent. So the existential creation contains no disparity.

Disparity arises only through this creation, since the Creator, glory be to Him, did not create readiness for it. Thus disparity arises in it from the absence of creation, not from creation itself. So reflect on it.

What is attributed to the Lord, glory be to Him, is creation.

As for nonexistence, it is not an agent of it. So if what would require the perfection and soundness of the limbs of a fetus in the womb, and their proper balance, does not become complete in its matter, disparity occurs in it. Likewise with plants.

**[Section: Mention of a ruqyah (healing incantation) that repels the evil eye]**

Among the ruqyah that repel the evil eye is what is reported from Abu Abdullah al-Saji, that during some of his journeys, for pilgrimage or for military campaign, he was riding a fine she-camel. In the caravan there was a man with the evil eye, who rarely looked at anything without destroying it. It was said to Abu Abdullah: "Protect your camel from the one with the evil eye." He said: "He has no way to my camel." The man with the evil eye was told of his words, so he watched for Abu Abdullah's absence, came to his baggage, looked at the camel, and it trembled and fell. Abu Abdullah came and was told that the one with the evil eye had struck it with the evil eye, and that it was as he saw. He said: "Show me him." He was shown, and he stood over him and said: "In the name of Allah, a restraint that restrains, a dry stone, and a burning ember. I return the eye of the one with the evil eye upon himself and upon the person he loves most: ﴿Look again, do you see any flaw? Then look again twice, the sight will return to you humbled and weary﴾ [al-Mulk: 3–4]."

Then the eyeballs of the one with the evil eye came out, and the camel stood up, with no harm upon it.

[Section: Sins corrupt the intellect]

Among them: sins corrupt the intellect. The intellect has a light, and sin inevitably extinguishes the light of the intellect; when its light is extinguished, it weakens and diminishes.

Some of the early Muslims (al-Salaf) said: No one disobeys Allah until his intellect departs from him. This is evident, for if his intellect were present, it would restrain him from disobedience, while he is in the grip of the Lord (Exalted is He), or under His subjugation, and He is watching over him, and he is in His house, on His carpet, with His angels as witnesses over him, looking at him. The preacher of the Qur'an forbids him, the preacher of death forbids him, and the preacher of the Fire forbids him. And what he loses through disobedience of the good of this world and the Hereafter is multiples of what he gains of pleasure and delight from it. So would one with a sound intellect embark upon treating all of that with contempt and making light of it?

(Benefit)

The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So they acknowledged their sin, so away with the companions of the Blaze﴾.

Allah, the Exalted, at times negates from these people intellect, hearing and sight, for they are the faculties of knowledge and the means of its acquisition; at other times He negates from them hearing and intellect; at other times He negates from them hearing and sight; at other times He negates from them intellect and sight; and at other times He negates from them only one of them.

So the negation of all three is a negation of the faculties of knowledge by way of direct correspondence (muṭābaqah), and the negation of some of them is a negation of them by direct correspondence, and of the others by implication (luzūm).

For when the heart becomes corrupt, hearing and sight become corrupt; indeed, the root of their corruption is the corruption of the heart. And when hearing and sight become corrupt, the heart becomes corrupt: when one turns away from hearing the truth and hates its speaker to the point that he does not love to see him, the arrival of guidance to the heart is prevented, and it becomes corrupt.

And when hearing and intellect become corrupt, the corruption of sight follows them. Thus each of these faculties is sound by the soundness of the others and becomes corrupt by their corruption. Therefore the Qur'an comes with the negation of that explicitly and by implication.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 67, verse 13–14:

This is among the most eloquent of proofs, for the Creator must know His creation, and the Maker knows what He has made. If you affirm that He is your Creator, the Creator of your breasts (ṣudūr) and of what they contain, then how could it be hidden from Him when it is His creation?

This proof is difficult for the Qadariyya (the Qadariyya) to grasp, for in their view He did not create what is in the breasts, so on their principles there was no evidence in the verse for His knowledge of it. For this reason the extremists among them pushed the matter to its conclusion and denied His knowledge, and so the early scholars (al-salaf) declared them unbelievers, all of them.

This proof drawn from the verse is sound under both readings, namely whether (man) (مَن) is in the nominative position as the subject (al-fā'iliyya), or in the accusative position as the object (al-maf'ūliyya).

On the first reading: Would the Creator, whose nature is creating, not know?

On the second reading: Would the Lord not know His creation and His making?

Then He concluded the argument with two names that necessitate its affirmation: al-Laṭīf (the Subtle), whose craftsmanship and wisdom are so subtle and fine that minds fall short of grasping them; and al-Khabīr (the All-Aware), whose knowledge reaches the comprehension of the inner reality and hidden depths of things, just as it encompasses their outer appearances.

How, then, could what the hearts contain and the breasts conceal be hidden from the Subtle, the All-Aware?!

He said in Shifā' al-'Alīl:

Among that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And keep your speech secret or declare it; indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts. Should He not know, He who created? And He is the Subtle, the Acquainted.﴾ (67:13–14)

Dhāt al-ṣudūr (what is within the breasts) is a phrase for what the breast contains of beliefs, intentions, love and hatred; that is, "possessor of the breasts," since these things are in the breasts and subsist in them, so they are ascribed to them by way of companionship and inherence.

There is a difference of opinion regarding the i'rāb (grammatical analysis) of (man khalaqa) (مَن خلق): is it in the nominative or the accusative?

If it is nominative, then it is an argument for His knowledge of that, by virtue of His creating it, and the sense is: He knows what the breasts contain; and how could the Creator not know what He created?

This argument is utterly clear and sound, for creating entails the living, powerful, knowing and willing nature of the Creator.

If it is accusative, the meaning is: Should He not know His creation?

The word (man) (مَن) is mentioned in a generalizing manner (taghlīban) so that it encompasses the rational knower and his attributes under both readings. The verse therefore indicates both that what is in the breasts is created, and that He, glorified is He, knows it.

Moreover, He, glorified is He, created what is in the breasts as evidence of His knowledge of it, so He said: ﴿Should He not know, He who created?﴾ That is: how could what is in the breasts be hidden from Him when He is the One who created it? Had that not been created by Him, the argument for His knowledge from it would collapse. Thus His creating a thing is among the greatest proofs of His knowledge of it. When creating is negated, the proof of knowledge is negated, and nothing remains to indicate His knowledge of what the breast harbours, if He were not the Creator of it.

This is among the greatest disbeliefs in the Lord of the worlds, and a denial of what all the messengers, from the first to the last, agreed upon; and it is known by necessity that they conveyed to their peoples that He is one God with no partner, just as they conveyed to them the same.

(Exhortation)

Abū Asmā' said: A man entered a thicket and said: "If I were alone here committing disobedience, who would see me?"

Then he heard a voice that filled the space between the two lava-plains of the thicket: ﴿Should He not know, He who created? And He is the Subtle, the Acquainted.﴾

(A Great Benefit)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who made the earth subservient to you, so walk in its shoulders and eat of His provision; and to Him is the resurrection.﴾

He, glorified is He, informs that He made the earth ṣalūl (docile, submissive), yielding to being trodden upon, dug, cleft, and built upon, and He did not make it difficult or resistant to whoever wishes to do that with it.

And He, glorified is He, informs that He made it a cradle (mihād), a bed (firāsh), a carpet (basāṭ), a place of settlement (qarār), and a receptacle (kifāt).

And He informs that He spread it out (daḥāhā), flattened it (ṭaḥāhā), brought forth from it its water and its pasture, fixed it firmly with mountains, laid out in it the wide passes and roads, caused rivers and springs to flow in it, blessed it, and decreed in it its sustenance (aqwāt).

Among its blessings is that all animals and their provisions and sustenance come forth from it.

Among its blessings is that you deposit the grain in it and it brings it out for you many times over what it was.

Among its blessings is that it carries harm upon its back and brings forth for you from its belly the best and most beneficial things, so it conceals from you every ugliness and brings forth for you everything beautiful.

Among its blessings is that it covers the faults of the servant and the wastes of his body and hides them, embraces and shelters him, and brings forth for him his food and drink. So it is the thing that bears harm most and returns benefit most; there is nothing better than dust for him, further from harm and nearer to good.

The point is that He, glorified is He, made the earth for us like a docile camel which, however it is led, submits. The expression "its shoulders" (manākibihā) was used to mean its roads and passes, because of what preceded regarding its description as docile; the one walking upon it treads on its shoulders, which are the highest part of it. For this reason, manākib was explained as "mountains," like the shoulders of a human being, which are their upper parts.

They said: this is an indication that walking on its plains is easier.

Another group said: rather, the manākib are the sides and regions, and from this comes the "shoulders" of a person, meaning his sides.

What appears is that the intended meaning of manākib is the heights.

This is the face on which animals walk, the high part of the earth as opposed to the face opposite to it, for the surface of the sphere is its upper part, and walking occurs only on its surface. The expression with "shoulders" is apt because of what preceded regarding its description as docile.

Then He commanded them to eat of His provision which He deposited in it; He made it docile and easy for them, opened in it the paths and roads along which they walk, and deposited in it their provision. So He mentioned the preparation of the dwelling for benefit, moving about in it by going and coming, and eating of what He deposited in it for its inhabitants.

Then, by His saying ﴿and to Him is the resurrection﴾, He alerted that we, in this dwelling, are not settlers nor residents; rather we entered it as passersby, so it is not fitting that we take it as a homeland and a permanent abode. We entered it only to take provision from it for the abode of permanence. It is a station of passage, not a place of lasting joy; a crossing and a thoroughfare, not a homeland and a settled abode.

The verse thus includes the indication of His lordship, His oneness, His power and His wisdom and His kindness, the reminder of His blessings and His beneficence, and the warning against inclining toward this world and taking it as a homeland and abode, but rather that we hasten our journey in it toward His abode and His paradise.

So, within what this verse contains, is the knowledge of Him and His oneness, the reminder of His blessings, the urging to journey toward Him and to prepare for meeting Him and coming before Him, and the announcement that He, glorified is He, folds up this abode as if it had never been, and that He will bring its people back to life after He caused them to die: ﴿and to Him is the resurrection﴾.

(A Lesson)

Since the sustenance of the bird is by snatching, He did not give it teeth, because the time of plundering does not allow for chewing. He gave it a crop like a saddle-bag, into which it transfers what it seizes, and then it moves it to the gizzard at a time when it is able to do so. If it has chicks, it gives them their share before the transfer.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 67, verses 20–21:

Thus He (glory be to Him) combined victory and provision, for the servant is in need of one who repels his enemy by His victory and brings him benefits by His provision. He must therefore have a helper and a provider.

Allah alone is the One who grants victory and provides, for He is al-Razzaq (the Provider), dhu'l-quwwat al-matin (the Possessor of strength, the Firm). Among the perfection of the servant's discernment and knowledge is that he knows that if Allah afflicts him with harm, no one else can lift it from him, and if He bestows upon him a blessing, no one else can provide it to him.

It is related that Allah the Exalted revealed to one of His prophets:

"Acquire for Me subtle perceptiveness and hidden gentleness, for I love that."

He said: "O Lord, what is subtle perceptiveness?" He said: "If a fly alights on you, know that I am the One who caused it to alight, so ask Me to lift it from you."

He said: "And what is hidden gentleness?" He said: "When a grain comes to you, know that I am the One who brought it to mind for you."

Allah the Exalted has also said about the sorcerers: ﴿And they could not harm anyone thereby except by the permission of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102].

He, glory be to Him, alone is the One who suffices His servant, grants him victory, provides for him, and protects him.

Imam Ahmad said: Abd al-Razzaq related to us, Ma'mar informed us, he said: I heard Wahb say: Allah the Exalted said in some of His books:

"By My might, whoever holds fast to Me, even if the heavens with those in them and the earths with those in them plot against him, I will make for him a way out of that. And whoever does not hold fast to Me, I will cut off his hands from the means of the heavens, cause the earth to swallow him from beneath his feet, leave him suspended in the air, and then leave him to himself. My hand is full for My servant: when My servant is obedient to Me, I give him before he asks Me, and I respond to him before he calls upon Me, for I know best the need that is good for him."

Ahmad said: Hashim ibn al-Qasim related to us, Abu Sa'id al-Mu'addib related to us, from one who heard Ata al-Khurasani, who said: I met Wahb ibn Munabbih while he was circumambulating the House, and I said to him: "Narrate to me a hadith that I may memorize from you in this place, and be brief." He said: "Yes:

Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed to Dawud: 'O Dawud, by My might and My majesty, no servant of Mine who holds fast to other than Me, while I know that from his intention, will not be plotted against by the seven heavens and whoever is in them, nor the seven earths and whoever is in them, except that I will make for him an exit from among them. By My might and My majesty, no servant of Mine who holds fast to a created being other than Me, while I know that from his intention, will not do so except that I cut off the means of the heavens from his hand, make the earth unstable beneath his feet, and then I do not care in which valley he perishes.'"

This second aspect is more apparent to the common people than the one before it. For this reason they are addressed with it in the Qur'an more than the first, and it is to the first aspect that the messengers called.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 67, verse 30:

(From the copy of al-Qadi, from a part containing the explanation of verses of the Qur'an, from Imam Ahmad)

﴿Your water will sink away into the earth﴾. He said: "It cannot be reached by the bucket (al-rishaʾ)."

﴿Then who will bring you clear flowing water?﴾ He said: "On the surface of the earth."

I say: The explanation may take one of two meanings. The first is that maʿīn is a form on the pattern of faʿīl, from amʿana fi al-arḍ, meaning he went far into the earth.

The second is that it is a form on the pattern of maf‌ʿūl, from al-ʿayn, meaning something seen with the eye.

Its original form was maʿyūn, and then it underwent i'lal (morphological weakening/vowel-change) in the manner of mabīʿ and its paradigm.
